title: How Henri Picciotto Designs Great Lessons
author: Michael Pershan
summary: Pershan writes a personal, appreciative analysis of what makes Henri Picciotto's math teaching materials -- which he has used continuously since a chance online connection in 2011 -- work so consistently well across elementary, middle, and high school classrooms. His first identified design principle is a single set of instructions: activities like 'Clock Angles' or 'Map Coloring' give students one simple prompt rather than a scaffolded sequence of finicky sub-questions, which reduces the cognitive tax of reading new instructions and preserves the flow of the underlying mathematical puzzle. His second principle is 'heading towards generalization': activities like Number Pyramids are designed so a student only midway realizes they are inside a meaningful mathematical generalization, occasionally marked by a deliberate 'STOP sign' that forces a pause to reach for the pattern, reflecting Picciotto's belief (from his essay 'Nothing Works') that mathematical joy comes from the pleasure of understanding, not just from open discovery. His third principle is simply craftsmanship born of classroom experience: because Picciotto has personally taught elementary through high school, his materials are formatted to be classroom-ready -- contained to one or two pages, generous white space, built-in tables for organizing results, and discussion questions embedded for the teacher's use -- sparing other teachers the usual work of reformatting borrowed materials before they can use them. Pershan frames the whole piece as a tribute to a mentor whose combination of mathematical insight and genuine classroom teaching experience he considers rare and worth naming explicitly.
points: Pershan's first design principle is minimizing instructional overhead: a single simple prompt (rather than a scaffolded sequence of sub-questions) preserves the flow and challenge of a rich mathematical task, even though it costs some certainty that every sub-idea gets explicitly surfaced.

His second principle, 'heading towards generalization,' describes activities deliberately structured so a student discovers a mathematical pattern partway through rather than being told it upfront, sometimes marked by an explicit pause point ('STOP') to force reflection.

He identifies Picciotto's rare combination of qualities -- deep mathematical knowledge plus years of actually teaching elementary through high school students -- as the reason his materials are unusually classroom-ready: single-to-two-page formatting, generous white space, and built-in organizational tables and discussion prompts.

The piece implicitly makes a broader craft argument: materials designed by people without direct, sustained classroom teaching experience routinely need reformatting before they're usable, which Pershan frames as the default gap Picciotto's work closes.
quotes: It's not hard to imagine a more finicky version of this activity. "Draw 5:00." "Draw 5:30.

Where is the hour hand at 5:30?" and so on. This might help us feel confident that the student will encounter important ideas, but with a cost -- it's taxing to read new instructions, and it interrupts some of the fun and flow of the core puzzle.
One of my favorite essays by Henri is “Nothing Works.” He argues for non-dogmatism about teaching, as the job is too varied to allow for principled consistency.
These materials reflect a belief that what makes mathematics joyful isn't just discovery -- it's about the pleasure of understanding. This value comes through in much of his work.

I often find myself reformatting materials before class. I add white space. I clarify questions. I make new diagrams, or have to replace confusing contexts. This happens even more often with mathematically rich materials, as designers with command of advanced mathematics rarely also have experience teaching young children.

Henri, however, has taught elementary, middle, and high school students. His pages reflect a teacher’s perspective on curriculum design. Every activity is contained on one or two pages, so they print nicely.
I have no doubt that I’ll be drawing on Henri’s materials in my teaching next year, and for many years to come.
